paragraphs: Online learning involves making decisions repeatedly while learning from the results. This paper studies that setting when the available actions are very numerous. Earlier algorithms require a learning rate, a parameter whose choice affects performance. The authors identify setting that parameter well as an important practical obstacle, especially with a large action set.

Their contribution is a completely parameter-free algorithm for decision-theoretic online learning. They also introduce a new definition of regret, the criterion used to assess how well an online decision maker performs relative to alternatives. The new definition is intended to be more natural for applications involving many possible actions.

The algorithm performs well under the proposed regret criterion. Under earlier regret definitions, it also comes close to the best bounds available for previous algorithms with optimally chosen parameters. The significance is the combination: removing parameter tuning does not require abandoning strong comparisons with established methods, while the new evaluation criterion addresses the large-action setting directly.
neurips-2009-a-parameter-free-hedging-al.tldr: A parameter-free online learning algorithm approaches optimally tuned regret bounds while introducing a regret criterion suited to large action sets.

paragraphs: Regularization introduces preferences into statistical learning, and different preferences reflect different assumptions about a problem. This paper asks how the validity of those assumptions affects whether a regularizer succeeds. Its focus is smooth regularization in parametric models, examined through an asymptotic analysis that describes behavior as the amount of data grows.

The authors provide a unified framework for studying smooth regularizers. This matters because it connects the motivation for a regularization scheme with its statistical consequences. Instead of treating each scheme as a separate technique, the analysis offers a common way to understand how assumptions about the problem influence the value of the resulting regularization.

The analysis also motivates an algorithm for choosing regularization parameters, and that algorithm can itself be studied within the same framework. Applications include hybrid generative-discriminative learning and multi-task learning. The contribution therefore connects theoretical assessment with parameter selection across several learning settings, with conclusions framed by the paper's smoothness and asymptotic scope.
neurips-2009-asymptotically-optimal-regu.tldr: A unified asymptotic analysis connects the success of smooth regularizers to their underlying assumptions and motivates regularization parameter selection.

paragraphs: The two-sample problem asks whether two collections of observations come from the same distribution. This paper connects that question to learning a ranking that distinguishes the collections. Its starting observation is that, under the equal-distribution hypothesis, the optimal ROC curve has an area of one half.

The proposed test splits the data into two parts. One part trains a scoring function that is nearly optimal according to area under the ROC curve, or AUC. The function then assigns real-valued scores to observations in the remaining part. Ranking those scores turns the multivariate problem into a one-dimensional problem that can be tested with the standard Mann-Whitney Wilcoxon procedure.

The authors show that learning the scoring function preserves the test's consistency and power properties provided the resulting ranking is sufficiently accurate in AUC terms. That condition is central: the statistical argument depends on the quality of the learned ranking. A numerical experiment illustrates the method's efficiency, complementing the connection between predictive ranking and distribution testing.
neurips-2009-auc-optimization-and-the-tw.tldr: Learning an accurate AUC ranking on one data split enables a classical rank test on another to compare multivariate distributions.

paragraphs: Belief polarization occurs when people who initially disagree encounter the same evidence and each becomes more convinced of their existing position. This pattern is often interpreted as evidence of irrational reasoning. The paper examines whether the pattern itself is incompatible with Bayesian belief revision, a framework for updating prior beliefs in light of evidence.

The authors demonstrate that a variety of polarization cases can be consistent with a Bayesian approach. The central point is that observing the same evidence does not, by itself, establish that people with opposing prior beliefs must move toward agreement. Some forms of increasing disagreement can occur within the models considered.

Simulations indicate that polarization is relatively common within that particular class of Bayesian models, rather than merely possible in an isolated case. This qualifies the usual interpretation of the phenomenon: polarization alone need not demonstrate irrationality. The stated finding concerns compatibility with Bayesian updating and prevalence within the studied model class; it does not establish that every instance of human polarization is Bayesian.
neurips-2009-bayesian-belief-polarizatio.tldr: Belief polarization can be consistent with Bayesian updating and is relatively common within the model class studied.

paragraphs: A game-playing program uses a heuristic evaluation function to assess positions during search. This paper develops a way to improve that function using values produced by alpha-beta search. The idea is to train a relatively direct position evaluator toward the assessments obtained through deeper exploration of possible play.

The algorithm differs from earlier approaches in two stated ways. It updates the evaluator using every node in the search tree, rather than one node. It also takes the result of a deep search as its training signal, rather than waiting for the result of a subsequent search. Both choices determine how information generated by search becomes learning data.

The authors implement the method in the chess program Meep with a linear evaluation function. Starting from small random weights, Meep learns high-quality weights entirely through self-play. In online games against humans, it reaches master-level performance. The paper reports this as the strongest performance among chess programs whose heuristics were learned wholly through self-play, supporting the usefulness of deep-search assessments as training targets.
neurips-2009-bootstrapping-from-game-tre.tldr: Training a chess evaluator on deep-search values across all search-tree nodes enables Meep to learn master-level play through self-play.

paragraphs: Two people performing similar actions may differ in both timing and the spatial details of their movements. Aligning their recordings therefore requires more than matching corresponding timestamps. This paper introduces canonical time warping, or CTW, to align behavior between two subjects while accounting for temporal differences and variation within and between subjects.

CTW combines canonical correlation analysis with dynamic time warping. The combination brings together a way to relate the subjects' representations and a way to adjust their temporal correspondence. The method also extends canonical correlation analysis to allow local spatial deformations. These additions address differences in when an action occurs and how its observed form varies.

The authors evaluate CTW on synthetic data, motion-capture recordings of similar actions, and recordings of similar facial expressions. They report visually and qualitatively better alignment than leading techniques based on dynamic time warping. These findings support the value of handling spatial variation alongside timing differences in the tested behavior-alignment problems.
neurips-2009-canonical-time-warping-for-.tldr: Canonical time warping combines temporal alignment and local spatial deformation to improve alignment of similar human behaviors.

paragraphs: This paper asks when an optimal controller for a task can be assembled from simpler controllers. Each primitive is already a feedback controller pursuing its own objective. The proposed composition weights these primitives according to their progress toward their objectives and the compatibility of those objectives with the current task.

The resulting controller is provably optimal for a particular class of stochastic control problems. A defining feature of that class is that its Bellman equation can be transformed into a linear equation, even with nonlinear or discrete dynamics. This mathematical structure makes the composition possible; the optimality claim is conditional on belonging to that class.

For linear dynamics with Gaussian noise, the framework provides analytical solutions formed from nonlinear mixtures of linear-quadratic regulators, without requiring a quadratic final cost. More generally, it constructs primitives using singular value decomposition of the Bellman equation's Green's function. An illustration involving human arm movements shows how the framework can connect two prominent motor-control ideas: combining primitives and achieving task optimality.
neurips-2009-compositionality-of-optimal.tldr: For a specified class of stochastic control problems, appropriately mixing feedback-controller primitives produces a provably optimal task controller.

paragraphs: This paper presents a system for building a topological map from an image sequence. A central issue is loop closure: recognizing that images taken at different points in the sequence correspond to a place encountered before. Those repeated-place relationships provide information from which the system can construct a map of the environment.

The system introduces an image similarity score that considers both the appearance of local features and their relative positions. Dynamic programming matches images using those two kinds of information together. This makes spatial arrangement part of the comparison, alongside what the individual features look like, when assessing potential matches between images.

A Markov random field then models loop-closure probabilities, and loopy belief propagation finds a locally optimal labeling. The authors also outline how to turn the resulting loop-closure data into a topological map. Results cover four urban image sequences and one indoor sequence. The contribution connects image comparison, probabilistic loop-closure inference, and map construction within a single system.
neurips-2009-constructing-topological-ma.tldr: The system builds topological maps from image sequences by combining spatially informed image matching with probabilistic loop-closure detection.

paragraphs: Temporal-difference learning can become unstable when it uses nonlinear value approximators or learns from off-policy samples. Successful applications of conventional methods do not remove that possibility: their parameters may diverge. This paper extends an earlier gradient-based solution for linear approximation to smooth nonlinear approximators, including neural networks.

The authors introduce an objective related to Bellman error and two temporal-difference algorithms that optimize it through gradient descent. This provides a specific objective for the learning updates. The algorithms work incrementally, and their computational cost per iteration grows linearly with the number of parameters in the value approximator.

For finite Markov decision processes and smooth value approximators, the paper proves asymptotic almost-sure convergence under the usual stochastic approximation conditions. The algorithms are guaranteed to reach locally optimal solutions, so the result does not assert global optimality. The contribution is a conditional convergence foundation for nonlinear temporal-difference learning together with updates whose per-iteration cost scales directly with model size.
neurips-2009-convergent-temporal-differe.tldr: Two gradient-based temporal-difference algorithms converge to local optima with smooth value approximators under stated stochastic approximation conditions.

paragraphs: A topic model describes documents through distributions over vocabulary terms. This paper separates two aspects of those distributions: which terms belong to a topic, and how probability is distributed among the included terms. The proposed sparse topic model places that separation inside a nonparametric hierarchical Bayesian model of document collections.

Each topic has selector variables that identify its subset of the vocabulary. Smoothness is then modeled within that selected subset. This makes vocabulary membership an explicit part of the representation, allowing the model to distinguish topic sparsity from the distribution of probability across the words that remain.

The authors develop an efficient Gibbs sampler, including a general-purpose technique for sampling a Dirichlet mixture with a combinatorial number of components. They evaluate the model on four real-world datasets. Compared with traditional approaches, the reported results combine better predictive performance with simpler inferred models. The findings support explicitly modeling which words a topic can contain as a useful part of learning document representations.
neurips-2009-decoupling-sparsity-and-smo.tldr: A sparse topic model separates vocabulary selection from probability smoothing and achieves better prediction with simpler models on four datasets.

paragraphs: Transductive inference uses the relationship between training and test data when producing estimates for the test set. This paper builds on the idea that a good learner should produce matching output distributions on those two sets. The relationship is imposed at the level of distributions over outputs, providing a common principle for several prediction tasks.

The authors formulate this comparison as a classical two-sample problem: assess how two collections differ in distribution. They use distance measures in Hilbert space to handle that comparison efficiently in a general form. Distribution matching becomes the central mechanism of the resulting transduction algorithm.

The same algorithm can be used without modification for classification, regression, and structured estimation. This breadth matters because the organizing principle does not depend on one particular kind of output. The authors also show that several existing heuristics are special cases of their approach. The contribution thus offers both a shared algorithmic framework and an interpretation of earlier methods through the assumption of matching output distributions.
neurips-2009-distribution-matching-for-t.tldr: Matching training and test output distributions yields a transduction framework usable unchanged across classification, regression, and structured estimation.

paragraphs: Heavy-tailed models of natural-image gradients can provide useful prior information for restoring images. However, the resulting optimization can be nonconvex and too slow for large images. This paper develops a faster deconvolution method that retains a hyper-Laplacian prior while changing how the optimization is solved.

The method alternates between two phases. Its nonconvex phase separates into independent problems for individual pixels, which can be solved using a lookup table. For two particular parameter values, one half and two thirds, the authors also derive analytical solutions by finding roots of cubic and quartic polynomials, respectively.

Using either solution route, the reported method deconvolves a one-megapixel image in under approximately three seconds. It achieves quality comparable to existing methods such as iteratively reweighted least squares, reported to take approximately twenty minutes. This supports the claimed speed advantage in the demonstrated setting. The authors also describe the approach as extendable to related image-processing problems, while deconvolution is the application they demonstrate.
neurips-2009-fast-image-deconvolution-us.tldr: Separating nonconvex deconvolution into per-pixel subproblems delivers much faster restoration with quality comparable to existing hyper-Laplacian methods.

paragraphs: Nonparametric regression can struggle with high-dimensional data, but some regressors adapt to intrinsic dimension rather than the apparent size of the representation. This paper strengthens such results in a more general setting. It studies regression on a metric space, where distances provide the structure needed to relate inputs.

The proposed regressor combines aspects of tree-based regression and kernel regression. It produces a smooth function while requiring only O(log n) time to evaluate, where n is the sample size. These properties bring together smooth predictions and a prediction cost that grows logarithmically with the amount of data.

The authors derive a tight convergence rate of n raised to the power −2/(2+d), where d is the input space's Assouad dimension. The relevant dimension in this guarantee is therefore the specified geometric dimension of the space. The contribution links that dimension-dependent statistical rate with smoothness and fast evaluation in one regressor, extending the setting in which intrinsic-dimensional adaptation can be established.
neurips-2009-fast-smooth-and-adaptive-re.tldr: A regressor combining tree and kernel ideas provides smooth predictions, logarithmic evaluation time, and a tight rate governed by Assouad dimension.

paragraphs: Visual bag-of-words methods represent images using a dictionary of visual patterns. Sparse coding can express each local descriptor with only a few dictionary words, yet an entire image may still use many words. This paper addresses that distinction between sparsity of individual descriptors and sparsity of the complete image representation.

The authors use mixed-norm regularization to encourage both sparse image representations and a small overall dictionary. The approach can also encourage images from the same class to use the same dictionary words. In that configuration, class membership helps shape the representation by promoting shared vocabulary within a class.

Experiments on a benchmark image-classification dataset show better mean average precision when compact image representations or compact dictionaries are needed for computational efficiency. The finding is tied to that compactness requirement. The contribution is a way to control sparsity at the level relevant to storing and processing whole images, with an additional mechanism for incorporating class information into dictionary use.
neurips-2009-group-sparse-coding-2fad5d1.tldr: Group sparse coding encourages compact image representations and dictionaries, improving reported classification precision when compactness is required.

paragraphs: Recognizing an object again and deciding how many distinct objects have been encountered are closely related problems. A new observation might be another appearance of a familiar object or an encounter with a different one. This paper presents a simple statistical model to help explain how people make those judgments.

The authors evaluate the model in three behavioral experiments. The first suggests that prior knowledge influences whether people judge an observed object token to have been encountered before. Here, the important distinction is between an individual observation and the underlying object that may account for several observations.

The second and third experiments suggest that people can estimate how many objects they have seen and learn categories and their properties despite uncertainty about object identity. This means that category learning and object counting can proceed even while some observations remain ambiguously matched. The findings support a statistical account in which uncertainty about repeated encounters coexists with broader learning about the objects in an environment.
neurips-2009-individuation-identificatio.tldr: A statistical model and three behavioral experiments examine how people recognize repeated objects and learn despite uncertainty about identity.

paragraphs: Learning a distance function lets side information shape what a system treats as similar. Conventional Mahalanobis approaches use a fixed metric across the input space and require a matrix whose size grows quadratically with dimensionality. This paper targets both the computational burden and the difficulty of representing heterogeneous data with one fixed metric.

The proposed method learns nonlinear Bregman distances through a nonparametric scheme resembling support vector machines. A convex function generates the distance, and its Hessian implicitly determines the local metric. Because that local metric comes from the function's curvature, the method avoids assuming the same metric everywhere in the input space.

The authors provide an efficient learning algorithm and evaluate it through semi-supervised clustering experiments. They report better performance than leading distance-learning approaches and computational efficiency on high-dimensional data. These empirical results support the proposed combination of local flexibility and efficient learning. The central contribution is a learned distance representation that can vary across the space while incorporating side information.
neurips-2009-learning-bregman-distance-f.tldr: Learning nonlinear Bregman distances provides locally varying metrics and improves reported semi-supervised clustering performance on high-dimensional data.

paragraphs: Matrix factorization represents observed data through interacting factors, and constraints influence the kinds of features those factors can express. This paper presents a general Bayesian approach to probabilistic factorization subject to linear constraints. It combines a Gaussian observation model and Gaussian priors with bilinear equality and inequality constraints.

The authors develop an efficient inference procedure based on Gibbs sampling, a Markov chain Monte Carlo method. The framework includes Bayesian versions of nonnegative matrix factorization and factor analysis as special cases. This places several familiar factorization approaches within a broader probabilistic treatment of constrained models.

Evaluation focuses on a blind source separation problem. The resulting features are reported to be meaningful and interpretable, while differing substantially from features obtained with related factorization techniques. The stated result emphasizes the character of the recovered features rather than a universal ranking of methods. It illustrates how the constrained Bayesian formulation can produce a different, interpretable account of structure in the observed data.
neurips-2009-linearly-constrained-bayesi.tldr: A constrained Bayesian matrix-factorization framework uses Gibbs sampling to recover distinctive, interpretable features in a blind source separation problem.

paragraphs: Useful image features often need to remain stable when properties such as illumination or viewing angle change. Evaluating an unsupervised representation only through a classifier can make that stability difficult to assess directly. This paper proposes empirical tests that measure how invariant learned features are to different image transformations.

The tests examine a property of the representation itself: how much it changes under transformations that can confound vision tasks. This provides a way to study learned features without relying solely on their role in a classification system. The authors report that their performance metrics agree with existing measures of invariance.

In the deep autoencoders studied, deeper representations become invariant to increasingly complex transformations. This empirical finding supports the use of depth for learning such invariances in those models. The contribution includes both evidence about the representations and evaluation tools that can be applied to future unsupervised learning methods, making transformation stability a directly assessable part of their behavior.
neurips-2009-measuring-invariances-in-de.tldr: Direct empirical invariance tests show that deeper autoencoder representations tolerate increasingly complex image transformations.

paragraphs: Freely supplied annotations do not always describe the content they accompany. In social bookmarking and similar settings, this creates noise when annotations are used to learn about documents or images. This paper proposes a probabilistic topic model that separates content-related annotations from annotations unrelated to the content's meaning.

The model jointly generates content and annotations. It assumes that an annotation comes either from the topics responsible for the content or from a general distribution independent of that content. These two possible origins give the model an explicit way to represent the difference between semantically relevant annotations and background annotation noise.

The authors demonstrate the method using synthetic data and real social annotations for text and images. Extracted content-related annotations could serve as preprocessing for tasks such as text classification and image recognition, or help information retrieval. The contribution is a probabilistic treatment of relevance within the annotation model itself, with experiments supporting its effectiveness on the supplied types of annotation data.
neurips-2009-modeling-social-annotation-.tldr: A topic model separates content-related annotations from background noise by modeling two possible sources for each annotation.

paragraphs: Relational data records connections between entities, such as friendships in a social network. Predicting those connections requires a model of the hidden structure underlying them. This paper moves beyond latent class models, which describe entities through class membership, toward latent features that provide a richer representation of each entity.

The approach uses nonparametric Bayesian modeling to infer how many hidden features are needed while also learning which entities possess each feature. These are parts of the same inference problem. The representation can describe entities through combinations of features, expanding the kinds of latent structure available for predicting links.

The authors report improved link prediction on three datasets and attribute the improvement to the approach's greater expressiveness. The result supports the usefulness of the feature-based representation in those evaluations. The contribution combines a richer account of entities with inference over the number of features, extending the nonparametric approach previously used to learn both class counts and class assignments.
neurips-2009-nonparametric-latent-featur.tldr: A nonparametric Bayesian model jointly learns latent features and their number, improving link prediction on three datasets.

paragraphs: Ranking systems are often trained by minimizing a loss but evaluated using measures such as NDCG or MAP. This paper analyzes the connection between those two quantities for Ranking SVM, RankBoost, RankNet, and ListMLE. It shows that their losses upper-bound errors defined from ranking measures, providing a theoretical link between training and evaluation.

The key construction treats ranking as a sequence of classification tasks. A weighted sum of their errors defines an essential loss. The authors prove that this quantity lies above the measure-based ranking errors and below the training losses of the methods studied. This chain of bounds explains how minimizing those losses controls an upper bound on evaluation error.

The proof also suggests modifications that tighten the training losses' bounds on ranking errors. Benchmark experiments show that these changes can improve ranking performance. The contribution therefore goes beyond explaining existing objectives: it uses the relationship between objectives and evaluation measures to guide changes that receive empirical support.
neurips-2009-ranking-measures-and-loss-f.tldr: Common ranking losses upper-bound measure-based errors, and tightening those bounds can improve empirical ranking performance.

paragraphs: This paper models bag-of-words documents using a family of two-layer undirected graphical models. Different members handle different document lengths while keeping the same number of binary hidden units. Their softmax visible units share weights to those hidden units, tying the family together through a common learned representation.

Each model expresses document probabilities as a product of topic-specific distributions. Precision comes from intersecting several broad topics, which allows the learned topics themselves to remain relatively general. The authors contrast this mechanism with selecting a single precise topic to generate each word, and provide efficient procedures for inference and learning.

The reported comparisons with Latent Dirichlet Allocation show substantially better generalization in held-out document log probabilities. The learned low-dimensional topic vectors also perform substantially better for retrieving documents similar to a query document. These findings support both the model's probability estimates and its usefulness as a document representation, with the product-based combination of topics central to the proposed explanation.
neurips-2009-replicated-softmax-an-undir.tldr: Replicated Softmax combines broad topics through a product model and reports better document modeling and retrieval than LDA.

paragraphs: When variables measure locations on shapes, trajectories, or images, their arrangement carries useful information. Sparse graphical models keep only selected probabilistic dependencies, but sparsity alone does not express local regularities in those dependencies. This paper introduces Gaussian graphical models that encourage both sparse structure and local constancy.

The model uses an l1-norm penalty to impose these structural preferences. The authors also develop an efficient algorithm that breaks a strictly convex maximum-likelihood estimation problem into a sequence of subproblems with closed-form solutions. The approach therefore addresses both what structure should be learned and how to estimate it.

Synthetic experiments assess recovery against known ground truth, while real-data experiments examine generalization. Reported examples capture heart rotation and shrinking, correlations between body parts during walking, and interactions among brain regions. The method outperforms leading Gaussian graphical structure-learning techniques on both small and large datasets in the reported evaluations. These findings support using locality alongside sparsity when modeling structured measurements.
neurips-2009-sparse-and-locally-constant.tldr: Gaussian graphical models that encourage both sparsity and local constancy recover useful structure and improve reported generalization.

paragraphs: A learned distance matrix determines how differences between data points contribute to their separation. This paper develops a model that learns such a matrix while also reducing dimensionality. The two goals are handled together through a sparse representation, rather than treating the choice of representation as a separate preliminary step.

The representation uses a mixed-norm regularizer that is nonconvex in its initial formulation. The authors show that the problem has an equivalent convex saddle-point, or min-max, formulation. This reformulation is the bridge to an efficient smooth optimization approach, even though the learning model uses a nondifferentiable loss.

The resulting optimization approach has an O(1/ℓ²) convergence rate, where ℓ is the iteration count, described as optimal for smooth problems. Experiments across several datasets evaluate the model's effectiveness and efficiency. The contribution links joint dimensionality reduction and distance learning to a tractable optimization formulation, with a stated convergence rate and empirical validation of the resulting method.
neurips-2009-sparse-metric-learning-via-.tldr: An equivalent convex saddle formulation enables efficient smooth optimization for jointly learning a sparse distance matrix and reducing dimensionality.

paragraphs: This paper proposes a model of natural-image statistics that actively seeks a simple form of dependence between components. The dependence has a tree structure, and the model learns both that structure and the image filters. Its aim differs from approaches that try to make the learned components statistically independent.

After learning from natural images, the resulting filters detect edges, resembling the filters associated with independent component analysis on natural images. This observation matters because a dependence-seeking model arrives at a similar kind of image feature. The learned edge structure therefore appears within this alternative statistical organization of the components.

Computing the model's likelihood requires estimating squared outputs for filter pairs joined in the tree. The authors observe that learned pairs predominantly share orientation while differing in phase. Their joint energy resembles models of complex cells. The findings connect the learned tree relationships to structured combinations of edge filters, while describing that biological connection as a resemblance rather than an identity.
neurips-2009-the-tree-dependent-componen.tldr: Learning tree-dependent natural-image components produces edge filters whose paired energies resemble complex-cell models.
